According to Chapter V (Applications), if a bridge has been ascertained to be unsafe and there is no time to warn the person, a public officer or anyone else may seize him and turn him back [1]. This does not really infringe his liberty, because liberty consists in doing what one desires, and he does not desire to fall into the river [1]. However, when there is not a certainty but only a danger of mischief, no one but the person himself can judge the sufficiency of the motive prompting him to incur the risk, so he ought only to be warned, not forcibly prevented — unless he is a child, delirious, or in some state incompatible with the full use of the reflecting faculty [2]. Finally, Mill says the principle of liberty applies only to human beings in the maturity of their faculties: not to children or young persons below the legal age, who must be protected against their own actions as well as external injury [3].

1st edition (1859) - elephant estimate: breeds at thirty years old, breeds till ninety, bringing forth three pair of young; at the end of the fifth century there would be alive fifteen million elephants descended from the first pair.
6th edition (1872) - elephant estimate: breeds at thirty years old, breeds till ninety, bringing forth six young, and surviving till one hundred years old; after a period of from 740 to 750 years there would be nearly nineteen million elephants alive descended from the first pair.

Between editions, Darwin changed the assumption from "three pair of young" to "six young" and added the assumption that elephants survive till one hundred years old; the result changed from fifteen million elephants at the end of the fifth century to nearly nineteen million elephants after 740 to 750 years.

Mill - On Liberty: society's tyranny through prevailing opinion and feeling, imposing its ideas and practices as rules of conduct on dissenters by means other than civil penalties, penetrating deeply into the details of life and enslaving the soul itself.
Tocqueville - Democracy in America: the majority's unbounded power extends to the arbitrary authority of the magistrate, treating public officers as its passive agents, directing or reprimanding them at every instant.

Mill sees the greatest danger in social tyranny—society enforcing its own mandates on individual thought and conduct beyond legal means—while Tocqueville emphasizes the majority's control over those in power, making officials its servants and extending its sway through administration.
